title: Darwin, Wallace and the Shared Discovery
text:
Charles Darwin had worked on his theory of evolution by natural selection for twenty years without publishing it. In June 1858 a letter arrived at his house in Kent from Alfred Russel Wallace, a young naturalist collecting specimens in the Malay Archipelago. Enclosed was a short essay setting out almost exactly the same idea. Darwin was stunned. He wrote to his friend Charles Lyell that he had never seen a more striking coincidence, and that he would rather burn his whole book than have anyone think he had behaved in a paltry spirit.

Lyell and the botanist Joseph Hooker found a solution. On July 1, 1858, they presented Wallace's essay together with extracts from Darwin's earlier writings at the Linnean Society of London. Neither author was there: Wallace was on the other side of the world, and Darwin was mourning his baby son.

Wallace could easily have felt cheated. Instead he was generous for the rest of his life. He insisted the theory was Darwin's and in 1889 titled his own book on it Darwinism. Darwin later helped secure Wallace a government pension, and Wallace was a pallbearer at Darwin's funeral in 1882.
lesson: When credit could be disputed, choose generosity over grievance. Rivals who share honor fairly can end up as friends and allies instead of enemies.
people: Charles Darwin, Alfred Russel Wallace, Charles Lyell, Joseph Hooker
location: Down House, Kent, and Linnean Society, London, England
source: Darwin and Wallace, "On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties," Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society, Zoology 3 (1858); Alfred Russel Wallace, Darwinism (1889)
